Lessons.Title: Reason About Quotients
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 U03:L16 goal: estimate, compare above/below one and order positive quotients of a whole and a unit fraction without calculating first. Division direction matters; students justify comparison of dividend and divisor.
Warm-up How Many One Fifths? source 98÷1/5 is a little LESS than 100÷1/5=500 and is exactly 490; do not replace source with 97÷1/6 and an unrelated 600 estimate.

Activity 1 Greater Than or Less Than 1: six ACTUAL source expressions: 25÷1/5=125, 1/7÷25=1/175, 1/8÷25=1/200, 25÷1/7=175, 25÷1/8=200 and 1/5÷25=1/125. The three whole-dividend expressions are above one; the three unit-fraction-dividend expressions are below one.

Activity 2 Estimate and Divide: order the SAME six source expressions from least to greatest without computing: (1/8)÷25 < (1/7)÷25 < (1/5)÷25 < 25÷(1/5) < 25÷(1/7) < 25÷(1/8). Then choose two to calculate and justify exact values 1/200,1/175,1/125,125,175,200.

Original six-expression ordering and source comparison explanation remain TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED; exact numeric subskills are selected digital supports, not proof of reasoning. Independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down compares 30÷1/6 vs (1/6)÷30.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Quotients of opposite magnitudes
KeyConcepts.Definition: A positive whole divided by a proper unit fraction gives a result above one; a proper fraction divided among a positive whole count gives a result below one.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fixed whole, smaller divisor
KeyConcepts.Definition: The number of small groups grows when their positive unit-fraction size decreases.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For fixed n>0 and b<c, n÷1/b<n÷1/c.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fixed integer divisor, smaller fractional dividend
KeyConcepts.Definition: A smaller positive fractional starting amount gives a smaller equal share.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source estimation 98 fifths
WorkedExamples.Question: Estimate and compute 98÷1/5 compared with 100÷1/5.
WorkedExamples.Method: One whole has five one-fifths groups.
Steps: 98 is two fewer whole units, so 10 fewer fifth-sized groups.
Result 490, a little less than 500.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source classify six quotients around one
WorkedExamples.Question: Which source 25/one-fraction quotients are larger than 1?
WorkedExamples.Method: Distinguish whole count divided into small groups from a small fraction shared among 25.
Steps: 1/7÷25,1/8÷25,1/5÷25 yield fractions less than 1.
Keep original fraction dividend and whole divisor positions.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source ascending order
WorkedExamples.Question: Order six original source expressions from least to greatest.
WorkedExamples.Method: Reason conceptually before using exact values.
Steps: Within fractional results, 1/200<1/175<1/125.
All three fractions are below all three integers.
Among integer quotients 125<175<200.
WorkedExamples.Check: Do not insert unrelated 12-based source claims.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Sort without evaluating all quotients
WorkedExamples.Question: Classify 12÷1/3,12÷1/5,1/3÷12,1/5÷12 relative to one.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party, explicitly labeled mathematical representation with independent arithmetic check.
Steps: For whole divided by unit fraction, count many small fractions in each whole; values are greater than one.
For a unit fraction divided among twelve, the resulting share is smaller than the unit fraction and below one.
Use those meanings to group, then verify with independent mathematics.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 12÷1/3 and 12÷1/5 are above one; 1/3÷12 and 1/5÷12 are below one.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Order six quotient expressions
WorkedExamples.Question: Put 12÷1/3,12÷1/5,12÷1/8,1/3÷12,1/5÷12,1/8÷12 in increasing order.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party, explicitly labeled mathematical representation with independent arithmetic check.
Steps: Place all three fractional-dividend quotients before the whole-dividend quotients.
Among the small shares, the one-eighth divided among twelve is smallest.
Among whole-dividend quotients, the one-eighth divisor yields the most groups.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Bound a large quotient
WorkedExamples.Question: Estimate 97÷1/6 without first calculating an exact long expression.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party, explicitly labeled mathematical representation with independent arithmetic check.
Steps: Compare 97 with 100, which is slightly greater.
Each whole contains six sixths, so 100÷1/6=600.
Conclude 97÷1/6 is slightly below 600 and verify.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A sensible estimate is a little less than 600; exact value 582.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume every quotient is smaller than its dividend
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A positive divisor less than one increases the quotient.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Interpret division as counting tiny groups instead of an unqualified rule about shrinking.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reverse the conceptual ordering when changing denominator
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Larger denominators make unit fractions smaller and whole÷unit-fraction quotients larger.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare group size and number of groups before sorting.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original printed 2021 source uses 25 and warmup 98÷1/5, changing the values changes comparison tasks.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restore all six source 25 expressions and source 490 warmup, keep other examples only as extension.

SummaryPoints: Source six expressions all use 25 with 1/5,1/7,1/8.
Three quotients exceed one, three fall below one; explanations teacher reviewed.

Visuals.Title: Original source six expressions and comparison to one
Visuals.Description: First-party tabulated original source equations, with human review of no-calculation ordering explanations.

Lessons.Title: Fraction Multiplication and Division Situations
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 U03:L17 purpose: solve multiplication and division situations with fractions, choose the correct operation and original unit, and communicate needed facts. The source includes an information-gap partner card exchange not reducible to a single numeric question.
Warm-up original source Number Talk: 5÷1/6=30, 5×1/6=5/6, (1/5)÷6=1/30 and (1/5)×(1/6)=1/30. The latter two share a numerical result but have different operations and situational interpretations.

Activity 1 Info Gap: Tiles (source problem card/data card): the teacher gives separate cards and students may ask only for the measurements or facts needed to solve; the data card partner must not solve for them. Since original gated card contents are not verified, do NOT invent tile dimensions, areas or fixed source answer. Provide original source procedure, a separate teacher-authored optional prompt and a teacher rubric for information requested and mathematical reasoning.

Activity 2 source real-life questions: 11 grains of rice weigh 1/3 gram, so each grain weighs 1/33 gram; Mai runs 3/4 of a 9/10-mile road, covering 27/40 mile; each tennis ball weighs 2 1/16 ounces and nine balls weigh 297/16 = 18 9/16 ounces. Students name their operations, models and units in each response.

Exact numeric selected Practice supports source warm-up and three public Activity2 arithmetic cases. The original tile information gap, partner dialogue, any original card figures and qualitative explanations remain TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED; independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down assesses choice of operation and an original full-whole model.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Area of one fractional tile
KeyConcepts.Definition: The tile's area is the product of its two perpendicular fractional lengths.
KeyConcepts.Example: Each tile covers one eighth of one square foot.

KeyConcepts.Title: Grid counting without overlaps
KeyConcepts.Definition: A rectangular floor can be covered by rows×columns of congruent tiles when side lengths divide evenly.

KeyConcepts.Title: Information-gap assessment
KeyConcepts.Definition: No unique tile count exists without knowing tile dimensions or area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Ask for the missing tile size and justify why it is needed before calculating.
KeyConcepts.Example: Different tile sizes change the required count on the same floor.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source rice grains equally shared mass
WorkedExamples.Question: If 11 grains of rice weigh 1/3 gram total, how much does one grain weigh?
WorkedExamples.Method: Divide a fraction of a gram among eleven equal grains.
Steps: Original unit is one gram.
The rice sample weighs one third gram total.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source Mai road fraction
WorkedExamples.Question: Mai runs 3/4 of her 9/10-mile road. How many miles?
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply positive fractions of original road length.
Steps: Full road measures 9/10 mile.
Multiply 9/10 by 3/4.
Distance traveled is 27/40 mile.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source tennis ball mass
WorkedExamples.Question: Nine balls each weigh 2 1/16 ounces. Find combined mass.
Steps: 2 1/16 = 33/16 ounces each.
Nine times 33/16 = 297/16 ounces.
WorkedExamples.Check: Nine balls weigh just above 18 ounces, consistent with about 2 oz each.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Missing tile dimensions
WorkedExamples.Question: A floor is 2 ft by 1 1/2 ft, but tile dimensions are hidden. Can the exact count be known?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party, explicitly labeled mathematical representation with independent arithmetic check.
Steps: Calculate floor area 2×1 1/2=3 square feet.
Recognize that smaller tiles require more pieces and larger tiles fewer.
Ask the partner for tile length and width or an exact equivalent area plus layout constraints.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No exact tile count until tile dimensions are supplied.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks the request and the learner's explanation of necessity.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Fill a floor with congruent tiles
WorkedExamples.Question: Floor 2 ft×1 1/2 ft, tiles 1/4 ft×1/2 ft. How many fit without gaps?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party, explicitly labeled mathematical representation with independent arithmetic check.
Steps: Across 2 feet, count 2÷1/4=8 tile columns.
Along 1 1/2 feet, count (3/2)÷(1/2)=3 tile rows.
Multiply 8×3 and confirm compatible edge lengths.
WorkedExamples.Check: One tile is 1/8 ft²; 24×1/8=3 ft², the floor area.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — A second tile area problem
WorkedExamples.Question: A 6-square-foot wall is covered with tiles that each cover 1/4 square foot. How many ideal full tiles?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party, explicitly labeled mathematical representation with independent arithmetic check.
Steps: Treat six square feet as total target area.
Count quarter-square-foot groups inside six square feet.
Multiply 6×4.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 24 tiles in the ideal non-overlapping model.
WorkedExamples.Check: 24×1/4=6 square feet; real edge cutting may change purchase quantity.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Choose a tile count before the tile size is known
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Several tile dimensions can fill or partly cover the same floor, yielding different counts.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Ask for necessary dimensional information before answering.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Multiply both widths and lengths without validating the layout
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The tile count from area may not create a whole-tile fit in arbitrary dimensions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check the number of rows and columns, nonoverlap, and edge-cut assumptions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Replace source Info Gap Tiles with a guessed tile dimension or invented fixed area
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original source splits problem and data cards and teacher HTML doesn't reveal all original card numbers; unsupported guesses misrepresent the task.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Preserve real partner exchange with a teacher-provided original card, mark gated values unverified, and use separately labeled independent math examples.

SummaryPoints: Information Gap Tiles uses separate problem and data cards, teacher-led; source-specific values unknown.
Mai's 9/10-mile road three quarters =27/40 mile; nine 2 1/16 oz tennis balls =18 9/16 oz.
Teacher reviews request-for-information and source diagrams; selected digital choices are only arithmetic support.

Visuals.Title: Original Grade5 L17 arithmetic and source-unit choices
Visuals.Description: First-party numeric summary; original information-gap tile card facts remain unknown and teacher reviewed.

Cells: do not invent a source answer

Lessons.Title: Represent Situations with Multiplication and Division
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: choose and justify multiplication and division representations for realistic fraction contexts, distinguishing why the same numbers give radically different answers when their roles are reversed. The public 2021 lesson explicitly relates a division equation and a multiplication equation to one contextual drawing.
Warm-up: compare 3×1/10=3/10 with 1/10×3=3/10, then compare 1/10÷3=1/30 with 3÷1/10=30. Explain that order is reversible in multiplication but not generally in division.

Activity 1 — original neighborhood meal: a package has 3 pounds of beans and each serving needs 1/4 pound. Count 12 quarter-pound portions and write 3÷1/4=12 and 12×1/4=3. Contrast with one quarter of a pound shared among three people: 1/4÷3=1/12 pound, and 3×1/12=1/4.

Activity 2: present two separate tape diagrams — one representing three whole pounds subdivided into fourths, the other representing one selected fourth subdivided into thirds — and ask partners to match each to its proper division and multiplication equation. Encourage a written explanation of why the order of multiplication factors is flexible but division terms are not.

Assessment: the original source requires stories, diagrams, both operations and partner revision; numeric result can be checked, but drawings and equation-story correspondence require teacher review. Original publisher images and gated solutions are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Whole divided by unit fraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Count the number of small fixed-size servings.
KeyConcepts.Example: Three pounds supply twelve quarter-pound portions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit fraction divided by whole
KeyConcepts.Definition: Distribute one fractional amount into equal smaller portions.
KeyConcepts.Example: A quarter pound shared three ways gives each person a twelfth pound.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiplication and division relations
KeyConcepts.Definition: Division can be checked by multiplying quotient times divisor, but exchanging dividend and divisor changes the question.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If a÷b=q, then q×b=a when b is nonzero.

WorkedExamples.Title: Count servings
WorkedExamples.Question: Three pounds of beans, quarter-pound portions. How many servings?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party, explicitly labeled mathematical representation with independent arithmetic check.
Steps: Count four quarter-pound groups in each full pound.
Multiply 3×4=12.
Write the matching division and multiplication statements.

WorkedExamples.Title: Divide a quarter
WorkedExamples.Question: One quarter pound is shared by three students. What does each receive?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party, explicitly labeled mathematical representation with independent arithmetic check.
Steps: Mark a quarter of a whole pound.
Divide the selected quarter into three equal pieces.
Compare the pieces to all twelve equal parts of the full pound.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish equations with identical printed numbers
WorkedExamples.Question: Are 3÷1/4 and 1/4÷3 the same?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party, explicitly labeled mathematical representation with independent arithmetic check.
Steps: Interpret the first as counting quarter-pound servings in three pounds.
Interpret the second as dividing one-quarter pound among three people.
Find each and explain the different resulting units.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Conclude division is commutative because multiplication is commutative
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Swapping the dividend and divisor changes the number or size of groups.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Write the actual story roles and check with inverse multiplication.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use the same area diagram for opposite division expressions
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One model represents whole-group counting while the other represents fractional equal sharing.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Draw the correct original whole and identify the divided quantity before partitioning.

SummaryPoints: Related multiplication equations can verify a division calculation.
Whole÷unit fraction counts groups; unit fraction÷whole gives a smaller share.

Source: 2021 first-edition IM K–5 Grade 5 Unit 3 Lesson 18 https://im.kendallhunt.com/k5/teachers/grade-5/unit-3/lesson-18/lesson.html. Lessons.Title: How Much in the Group? (optional)
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: recover an unknown WHOLE from the exact size of a unit-fraction share and explain why different equations represent the same relationship. The public 2021 task uses class sizes and checks the meaning of each number and inverse operation.

Warm-up: consider an approximately shaded one-quarter of a bar with a marked part labelled 14. Estimate the total whole, distinguishing a plausible estimate near 56 from a uniquely exact computation only when the fraction one-quarter is explicitly given.

Activity 1 — original student-club context: one fourth of the fifth-grade students belong to a chess club, and that club has seven students. Build four equal seven-student groups to find total 28. Explain the three equivalent relationships: (1/4)×T=7, T÷4=7 and 4×7=T.

Activity 2: another club contains 12 students and represents exactly one third of the grade. The whole grade has 36 students; compare 1/3×36=12, 36÷3=12 and 3×12=36. Present and critique an incorrect candidate equation (1/3)÷12=T, explaining why it is an unrelated division of a unit fraction by a large whole.

Assessment: the source asks learners to select ALL contextual equations and justify why an inverse relationship reconstructs the whole; a numeric T=28 or T=36 is only supporting evidence. Students' modeling, estimation and explanation remain teacher-reviewed. Gated source images and original student response were not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Recover the whole from a unit share
KeyConcepts.Definition: If one of b equal shares of a whole is known, multiply that share by b to recover the total.
KeyConcepts.Example: One fourth of class is seven students, so whole class is 28.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent missing-factor equations
KeyConcepts.Definition: The relationships between total T and share s can use multiplication or division.

KeyConcepts.Title: Check a context-specific equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: An equation must represent how many identical shares make the whole.
KeyConcepts.Rule: An expression involving a fractional dividend may be valid arithmetic but irrelevant to the class-size story.
KeyConcepts.Example: (1/4)÷7 is not a class-size reconstruction equation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find the total grade
WorkedExamples.Question: One fourth of a class is seven students. What is the whole count?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party, explicitly labeled mathematical representation with independent arithmetic check.
Steps: Represent one quarter as seven students.
Build four equal seven-student groups.
Multiply 4×7.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare three correct equations
WorkedExamples.Question: Show three matching equations if one third of a grade has 12 students.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party, explicitly labeled mathematical representation with independent arithmetic check.
Steps: Rewrite as T÷3=12.
Use the inverse 3×12=T to find 36.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject an unmatched candidate
WorkedExamples.Question: Does 1/4÷7=T represent the whole when one fourth is seven students?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party, explicitly labeled mathematical representation with independent arithmetic check.
Steps: Interpret the dividend 1/4 as a fractional amount divided among seven.
Observe the quotient would be 1/28, a tiny share.
Compare with four equal groups of seven students yielding the whole 28.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No. The correct whole is 28 students, not 1/28.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews the explanation of which equation quantities correspond to students.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Divide the known one-fourth share by four to find the whole
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The known share is only one of four equal groups, so the whole is larger.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply by the number of equal groups to recover the whole.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Match an equation by its printed digits alone
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Fractions and whole-number counts play different mathematical roles.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Describe the context for each factor, dividend, divisor and missing value.

SummaryPoints: An exact unit-fraction share can determine the original whole using inverse multiplication.
Multiple equations can correctly describe the same class-size situation.
Teacher reviews selected-equation reasoning, estimates and interpretation of the original whole.
